INSY 2299 · Session 11
Understanding Software

Hardware – data storage types you NEED to know

Random Access Memory (RAM)

RAM is a temporary storage that fast access for executing computer programs and files.

The RAM inside a personal computer is volatile memory, meaning that when the power goes out, all is lost that wasn’t saved to nonvolatile memory (i.e., a more permanent storage media like a hard drive or flash memory).

Flash memory

Permanent storage, it is the chip-based equivalent of a hard drive.

It’s not as fast as the RAM used in most traditional PCs but holds data even when the power is off (nonvolatile memory).

Apple’s MacBook Air was one of the first commercial notebook PCs to offer flash memory. Flash memory is also used in USB drives, cameras and smartphones.

Try it: what survives a power outage?
or press →
INSY 2299 · Session 11
Class check

You edit a Word file for two hours without saving. The power goes out. What is lost?

Open programs and unsaved edits live in RAM, which is volatile. Saved files sit on nonvolatile storage (flash or hard drive) and survive. That is why autosave writes to disk every few minutes.

INSY 2299 · Session 11
Understanding Software

Two main types of software

Software
Operating Software

Software that controls the computer hardware

Establishes standards for developing (writing) and executing applications

Example: Operating Systems

Application Software

Desktop applications, enterprise software, utilities, and other programs that perform specific tasks for users and organizations

Example: Customer Relationship Management (CRM Salesforce) and Productivity Software (MS OFFICE)

or press →

Which of these is operating software, not application software?

Android controls the phone’s hardware and sets the standards that apps are written to. Excel, Salesforce, Spotify and Chrome perform specific tasks for users and run on top of an operating system.

Distributed Computing

Distributed computing – client-server architecture

Definition

Form of computing where systems in different locations communicate and collaborate to complete a task (e.g., delivering a website to a browser)

Click a client to send a request.

Server

Program that fulfills the requests of a client

Client

Software program that makes requests of a server program
Example: web browser, mobile app, ATM machine

INSY 2299 · Session 11
Distributed Computing

Multi-tiered distributed system

Company’s server systems
Clients
Smartphones
Computers
Web Server
Host and deliver websites to clients (smartphone, tablet, pc)
App Server
Software that houses business logic of multiple applications
Database
Stores data

Why a multi-tier architecture?

• Security (the database is not exposed to the Internet)

• Scalability (database clustering)

• Simple maintenance (web designer just works on the web server, the front-end)

• Easily upgrade/enhance (new databases as the company grows)

INSY 2299 · Session 11
Distributed Computing

Distributed computing – some more terminology

Web services

Software systems (small pieces of code) that are accessed via the application (app) server that enable communication between different systems over the internet. [Client <-> API <-> Server]

Example tasks:

  • Returning calculations
  • Accessing database programs
  • Making requests to another server in another organization

Example APIs:

  • Google Maps API: enables integration of maps into apps
  • Stripe API: provides payment processing capabilities
  • FedEx API: allows to calculate shipping rates
Try a shipping-rate call:

Request · app server → carrier

Response · carrier → app server

        
A toy rate table, not FedEx’s real prices or message format. The point: the shop’s app server asks another organization’s server and gets a number back.

Class check

  
The rule “a seat can never be sold twice” has to be enforced somewhere. Which tier?

  

    

      
      
      
      
      
    

    
Business rules belong in the app server: it checks the database for seats left before it writes a booking. A rule in the browser can be bypassed, and the web server only presents forms. The database stores the seat count; the app server decides what to do with it.

Software in Flux · Open Source

  
Open-source software (OSS)

  

    

      

        
Source code for OSS products is shared publicly.

        
  • Can be changed and redistributed by anyone.

        

          
In stark contrast to the practice of conventional software firms who:

          
  • Treat their intellectual property as closely guarded secrets.
  • Almost never provide the source code for their commercial products.

        

        
Seen by some firms as a threat that undermines their economic model.

Software in Flux · Open Source

  
Why open source?

  

    

      
Cost
Free alternatives to commercial code can be a tremendous motivator

      
Reliability
The more people who look at a program’s code, the greater the likelihood that an error will be caught and corrected

      
Security
“Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow”

      
Scalability*
Many forms of Open-Source Software (OSS) can be migrated to more powerful hardware.

      
Agility and time to market
Skip whole segments of the software development process (instead of developing in-house)

      
Discuss: “given enough eyeballs” – does that also hold for a small project with three volunteers?

    

    
or press →

    
*Ability to either handle increasing workloads or to have the potential to manage workload increases

    Class check
    
  
    MongoDB gives its database software away for free. Where does its ~$1B+ annual revenue come from?
    
  
    
    
    
      
      
      
      
      
    
    
    
    The software is free; running it is not. MongoDB charges for a managed cloud service, so customers pay to not run the servers themselves. Search partnerships are Mozilla’s model; open-source code by definition isn’t sold as a secret license.

    Differences SaaS, PaaS and IaaS
    
  
    
    
    Definition SaaS
    Software made available by a third party online (running on their server).
    
    
    PaaS and IaaS
    Utility computing: Firm manages its own applications and then runs it over the Internet on a service provider’s computers.
    
    
    Think about it: a firm develops its own software and then runs it over the Internet on a service provider’s computers. Which model is that, and who gets the call at 3 a.m. when the application crashes?

        Software in Flux · TCO
        
  
        Total costs of ownership (TCO)
        
  
        
    
        All the costs associated with any form of capital, including a software system of a product (purchase price + costs of operation)
        
    
        
      
        Direct costs
        Hardware, software purchase costs
        
      
        Indirect costs
        Ongoing administration costs, maintenance, upgrades, technical support, training, utility and real estate costs
        
      
        Hidden costs
        Support staff, downtime, …
        
    
        
    
        
      
      
        
        
        
        Four-year saving: 
        
        
        A higher sticker price can still mean a lower TCO: free software, lower support costs, higher resale value.

        Software in Flux · Virtualization
        
  
        Virtualization
        
  
        
    
          
      
        • A type of software that allows a single computer to function as if it were several different computers.
          • 
      
        • Each virtual computer can run its own operating system and software.
          • 
      
        • Examples: Server with different virtual machines or Mac with both OS and Windows installed (“Boot Camp”)
          •

        Software in Flux · Virtualization
        
  
        Why virtualization?
        
  
        
    
        Efficiency: you need fewer servers (save money)
        • Higher utilization while still meeting peak demand
        • Confront changing demand
        
    
        Simplified IT operations and management
        • Scalability* (can scale-up easily)
        • Can support “legacy systems” (backward compatibility)
        
    
        Bottom line
        • Flexibility
        • Cost savings (TCO)
        
    
        or press →
        
    
        *Ability to either handle increasing workloads (or to have the potential to manage workload increases)
        
  
        
  
        INSY 2299 · Session 11
        

        


        
  
        Software in Flux · Virtualization
        
  
        Fewer servers: how far can virtualization consolidate?
        
  
        
    
        
      
      
      
    
        
    
        Illustrative: workload = servers × average utilization; hosts = ROUNDUP(workload ÷ target utilization). Real sizing also checks memory and peak loads.
        
    
        
      
        Before: one application per server
        
      
        After: virtual machines packed onto hosts

        Servers retired
